title: Due Process and Regulatory Taking — Maplewood Homeowners Association v. City of Riverside
facts: The Maplewood Homeowners Association represents 340 homeowners in a residential subdivision in the City of Riverside. In January 2025, the City Council passed Ordinance 2025-47, which retroactively rezoned the Maplewood subdivision from R-1 (single-family residential) to MU-3 (mixed-use high density), allowing commercial development and apartment buildings up to 12 stories. The ordinance was passed under the state's new Housing Acceleration Act, which grants municipalities emergency rezoning authority to address housing shortages. The homeowners allege: (1) the rezoning constitutes a regulatory taking under the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause because it destroys the residential character and substantially diminishes property values (appraisals show 25-40% decline); (2) the retroactive application violates procedural due process under the Fourteenth Amendment because homeowners received only 72 hours' notice of the rezoning hearing, far below the 30-day requirement in the city's own charter; (3) the ordinance violates substantive due process because it bears no rational relationship to the housing shortage, as the subdivision is already fully developed with no vacant land. The City argues: (1) the rezoning is a valid exercise of police power under the Housing Acceleration Act; (2) no physical taking occurred and the diminution in value does not meet the Penn Central test threshold; (3) the abbreviated notice was authorized by the state emergency housing statute, which preempts local charter requirements; (4) the rational basis test is met because the rezoning allows densification through teardowns and rebuilds. The case raises unresolved constitutional questions about whether state emergency housing statutes can override municipal due process protections, and whether retroactive upzoning that destroys neighborhood character constitutes a regulatory taking — issues where state supreme courts have issued conflicting rulings.
supporting_materials: Ordinance 2025-47 full text with rezoning maps. Property appraisals from three independent firms showing 25-40% value decline. City charter Section 4.12 requiring 30-day notice for rezoning hearings. State Housing Acceleration Act text and legislative history. Meeting minutes showing 72-hour notice was provided. Comparable case data: Kelo v. City of New London (2005), Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City (1978), Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council (1992). Expert report on housing density analysis showing no vacant parcels in Maplewood. Declarations from 47 homeowners describing financial hardship. Conflicting state supreme court rulings on emergency rezoning authority.
